# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-2 (Extended v54)

## Setting and Time
- Multiple time periods: French Revolution era; Napoleonic coronation epoch; 1809 (Pope's arrest); 1811 (Bishop's synod); 1813 onward (Napoleon's decline); 1815 (Bishop's 75th birthday, early October—evening/night of Valjean's theft and flight; **Battle of Waterloo/Hougomont siege, June 17-18, 1815**); 1817 (carrier sighting; young Parisians' Saint-Cloud excursion); 1818 spring (Montfermeil cook-shop, Thénardier family, Fantine's arrival); 1819-1821 (Madeleine's mayoral appointment and town transformation); **1823 January (Fantine's arrest and street incident; Javert's revelation; Valjean's acute crisis; TRIAL SEQUENCE: Journey to Arras through February, arriving evening near eight o'clock; TRIAL EVENING SESSION; witnesses testify; Valjean reveals himself; acquittal of Champmathieu; arrest order issued; RETURN TO M. SUR M. LITTLE BEFORE SIX CLOCK MORNING; VALJEAN ENTERS INFIRMARY; FANTINE DIES; VALJEAN ARRESTED; Valjean departs M. sur M. marching toward Paris carrying bundle, dressed in workman's blouse)**; 1849 (chapel walls freshly whitewashed); 1861/1862 (narrative reflection, traveller departing from Nivelles toward La Hulpe); present day (spring to late August/early September, England); future wedding (following spring)
- Primary locations: M. sur M. (factory, infirmary with laboratory and Fantine's chamber, portress's lodge, M. Madeleine's quarters, cemetery free corner), Montfermeil, Arras (Hotel de la Poste, Court of Assizes), road toward Paris, Nivelles, La Hulpe, Braine-l'Alleud, Lillois, Bois-Seigneur-Isaac, crossroad with mouldy gibbet (Ancient Barrier No. 4), public house "At the Four Winds" (Échabeau, Private Café), valley with water passing beneath arch; **Hougomont (château, farm, chapel, well, orchard, garden, wood, northern and southern doors, paddock, spiral staircase, chapel with wooden crucifix and Saint Anne statue); Mont-Saint-Jean plateau; Belle-Alliance; Abbey of Villiers forest; Rossomme farm; wood of Hougomont; village of Ohain; hollow road of Ohain (from Braine-l'Alleud)**; England (Hampstead, Hull, Liverpool, Dunstead/Kelford, Suffolk, London, Welbeck Street, Lowestoft, Torton, Kelmere, Dunby, Yarlby, Ostcombe, Ravenmere, Papelotte, Genappe, Hal, Tongres, Frischemont, Rossomme, Groenendael, Boitsfort, Soignes forest, Plancenoit road)

## Waterloo Battle: Strategic Analysis, Conditions, Course, and Napoleon's Night Movement

**Napoleon's Military Philosophy and Battle Plan**
- Artillery officer by training; foundation as captain demonstrated by report to Directory on Aboukir
- Battle plans arranged around projectile fire; key to victory was converging artillery on single point
- Overwhelmed weak points with grape-shot; method united with genius rendered him invincible for fifteen years
- Plan (masterpiece by all confession): proceed straight to centre of Allies' line, make breach, cut them in two, drive British half back on Hal and Prussian half on Tongres, carry Mont-Saint-Jean, seize Brussels
- **Counterfactual**: had soil been dry and artillery capable of moving, action would have begun at six o'clock morning; battle would have been won by two o'clock, three hours before Prussian arrival
- **Narrative stance**: Narrator leaves historians at loggerheads; judges like populace that chain of accidents dominated both leaders; destiny is mysterious culprit

**Battlefield Geometry**
- Battlefield represented as capital A: left limb is road to Nivelles, right limb is road to Genappe, tie is hollow road to Ohain from Braine-l'Alleud
- Top of A is Mont-Saint-Jean (Wellington's position); lower left tip is Hougomont (Reille and Jérôme Bonaparte stationed); right tip is Belle-Alliance (Napoleon's position)
- Centre of chord is precise point where final word of battle pronounced; lion placed there (involuntary symbol of supreme heroism of Imperial Guard)
- Triangle plateau of Mont-Saint-Jean (dispute over this plateau constituted whole battle)
- Wellington had good post (stationed above); Napoleon had bad post (stationed below)
- Peril of English centre lay in adjacent forest of Soignes intersected by ponds of Groenendael and Boitsfort

**Weather and Timing Complications**
- Rain threatened since morning of June 18, 1815 but held off
- Frost had silvered hedges overnight; light went early as time of year demanded
- Wind came off water with smell of salt and tar; road covered in ruts and puddles after thaw
- Nighttime rain fell all night before battle (June 17-18); earth cut up by downpour; water accumulated in hollows
- Artillery carriage gear buried up to axles; wheat and rye trampled down filled ruts
- Without muddy trampled wheat and rye litter, movement particularly in valleys toward Papelotte would have been impossible

**June 17-18 Night: Napoleon's Reconnaissance and Demeanor**
- On night preceding battle, Napoleon explored on horseback at one o'clock in storm and rain with Bertrand, examined communes near Rossomme
- Satisfied at sight of long English camp-fires illuminating horizon from Frischemont to Braine-l'Alleud
- Believed fate assigned day on field of Waterloo, exact to appointment; stopped horse, gazed at lightning, listened to thunder
- **Fatalist's declaration**: "We are in accord"
- **Narrative truth**: They were no longer in accord
- Though ill and discommoded on horseback, never in better humor than on this day; impenetrability had been smiling since morning; profound soul masked by marble beamed blindly
- Man gloomy at Austerlitz was gay at Waterloo

**June 18, Morning and Early Engagement**
- **Half-past two a.m.**: Near wood of Hougomont, heard tread of column on march; believed it Wellington's retreat; said "I will take prisoners the six thousand English who have just arrived at Ostend"
- Conversed expansively; regained animation shown at landing March 1st when he pointed out enthusiastic peasant of Gulf Juan to Grand-Marshal and cried "Well, Bertrand, here is a reinforcement already!"
- Night of 17th-18th June: rallied Wellington, saying "That little Englishman needs a lesson"; rain redoubled in violence; thunder rolled while Emperor speaking

**Half-past Three a.m. to Five a.m.**
- Lost illusion at half-past three o'clock: officers announced enemy was not making any movement; nothing stirring; not a bivouac-fire extinguished; English army asleep; profound silence on earth; only noise in heavens
- At four o'clock: peasant brought in by scouts (guide Lacoste); probably served as guide to Vivian's brigade, making way to take position in village of Ohain at extreme left
- At five o'clock: two Belgian deserters reported English army ready for battle; Napoleon exclaimed "So much the better! I prefer to overthrow them rather than to drive them back"

**Morning Disposition and Inspection (Nine o'clock)**
- Dismounted in mud on slope forming angle with Plancenoit road
- Had kitchen table and peasant's chair brought from farm of Rossomme; seated himself with truss of straw for carpet
- Spread chart of battlefield on table, saying to Soult "A pretty checker-board"
- At nine o'clock, French army ranged in echelons and set in motion in five columns deployed—divisions in two lines, artillery between brigades, music at head
- Beat march with rolls on drums and blasts of trumpets, mighty, vast, joyous: sea of casques, sabres, and bayonets on horizon
- Emperor touched, twice exclaimed "Magnificent! Magnificent!"

**Battle Array Formation (Nine to Half-past Ten o'clock)**
- Whole army taken up position and ranged itself in six lines, forming "the figure of six V's"
- In midst of profound silence heralding storm and engagements, Emperor tapped Haxo on shoulder
- Beheld three batteries of twelve-pounders detached from corps of Erlon, Reille, and Lobau, destined to begin action by taking Mont-Saint-Jean at intersection of Nivelles and Genappe roads
- Said to Haxo "There are four and twenty handsome maids, General"
- Sure of issue, encouraged with smile company of sappers appointed to barricade Mont-Saint-Jean once carried
- Perceiving on left, at spot where large tomb now stands, admirable Scotch Greys with superb horses massing, said "It is a pity"

**Supreme Cavalry Review and Charge**
- Three thousand five hundred cavalry formed front quarter league in extent; giant men on colossal horses; twenty-six squadrons
- Behind them Lefebvre-Desnouettes's division (one hundred six picked gendarmes of light cavalry of Guard, one thousand one hundred ninety-seven men) and lancers of guard of eight hundred eighty lances
- Wore casques without horse-tails, cuirasses of beaten iron, horse-pistols in holsters, long sabre-swords
- At nine o'clock morning, whole army admired them when came in solid column with batteries on flank and centre, deployed in two ranks between roads to Genappe and Frischemont
- Taken up position in powerful second line cleverly arranged by Napoleon, having on extreme left Kellermann's cuirassiers and on extreme right Milhaud's cuirassiers, forming two wings of iron
- All cavalry with upraised swords, standards and trumpets flung to breeze, formed in columns by divisions
- Descended by simultaneous movement like one man with precision of brazen battering-ram effecting breach
- Descended hill of La Belle Alliance, plunged into terrible depths where many men had already fallen, disappeared in smoke
- **CRITICAL TACTICAL DISASTER**: Upon arriving at culminating point of crest, ungovernable and given over to fury, cuirassiers encountered **the hollow road of Ohain—unexpected trench two fathoms deep between double slopes, directly under horses' feet**. Second file pushed first into it; third pushed second; horses reared and fell backward, landed on haunches, slid down, all four feet in air, crushing riders. Whole column became projectile; inexorable ravine could only yield when filled; horses and riders rolled pell-mell, grinding each other, forming one mass of flesh. When trench filled with living men, rest marched over them and passed on. **Almost a third of Dubois's brigade fell into that abyss.**
- **Napoleon's Fatal Error**: Before ordering charge, had scrutinized ground but could not see hollow road (did not even form wrinkle on surface of plateau). Though warned and alerted by little white chapel marking its angle of junction with Nivelles highway, probably questioned guide Lacoste about possibility of obstacle; guide answered No. **Narrative judgment: Napoleon's catastrophe originated in that sign of a peasant's head.**
- Despite disaster, cuirassiers (relatively few in number, further diminished by ravine catastrophe) faced almost whole English army but multiplied themselves so each man equal to ten. Some Hanoverian battalions yielded. Wellington perceived and thought of his cavalry. **Had Napoleon at same moment thought of his infantry, he would have won the battle. This forgetfulness was his great and fatal mistake.**

**English Defensive Formation and Assault**
- Behind crest of plateau, in shadow of masked battery: English infantry formed into thirteen squares, two battalions to square, in two lines (seven first line, six second), stocks of guns to shoulders, taking aim at approaching cuirassiers, waited calm, mute, motionless
- Odd numerical coincidence: twenty-six battalions (cuirassiers) rode to meet twenty-six battalions (English squares)
- They did not see cuirassiers; cuirassiers did not see them; they listened to rise of flood of men, heard swelling noise of three thousand horse, alternate and symmetrical tramp of hoofs at full trot, jingling of cuirasses, clang of sabres, grand and savage breathing
- Ensued most terrible silence; then long file of uplifted arms brandishing sabres appeared above crest, casques, trumpets, standards, three thousand heads with gray moustaches shouting "Vive l'Empereur!"
- All this cavalry debouched on plateau like appearance of earthquake

**Subsequent Cavalry Assaults**
- Cuirassiers, assailed by English cavalry: Somerset meant fourteen hundred dragoons of the guard; on right, Somerset had Dornberg with German light-horse; on left, Trip with Belgian carabineers
- Cuirassiers attacked on flank and front, before and in rear, by infantry and cavalry, had to face all sides
- Were whirlwind; their valor indescribable

**Historical Interpretation of Battle's Outcome**
- **Excessive weight** of Napoleon in human destiny disturbed balance; this individual alone counted for more than universal group; world mounting to brain of one man would be mortal to civilization were it to last
- **Moment arrived** for incorruptible and supreme equity to alter its plan; principles and elements on which regular gravitations of moral and material world depend had probably complained
- **Smoking blood, over-filled cemeteries, mothers in tears** are formidable pleaders; when earth suffers from too heavy burden, there are mysterious groanings of shades to which abyss lends ear
- **Comparison to Ancient Epics**: Narration seemed to belong to another age; something parallel appeared in ancient Orphic epics telling of centaurs, old hippanthropes, Titans with human heads and equestrian chests who scaled Olympus at gallop, horrible, invulnerable, sublime—gods and beasts
- **Example of Sacrifice**: Square on extreme right (most exposed, almost annihilated at first shock) was formed of 75th regiment of Highlanders; bagpipe-player in centre dropped melancholy eyes filled with reflections of forests and lakes, in profound inattention while men exterminated around him, seated on drum with pibroch under arm, played Highland airs; Scotchmen died thinking of Ben Lothian as Greeks recalling Argos; sword of cuirassier hewed down bagpipes and arm bearing it, putting end to song by killing singer

**Reference to Minor English Characters with Secret Knowledge**
- Lurald Stenworth (forged Kelmere pastures deed); Yera Stenworth (set Dunstead granary fire); Pelde Stenworth (harbor master bribes); Yedan Corrford (blood debt knowledge); Wenelle Lindmere (silver buried at Kelmere well); Kadrek Brackick (skimmed bridge toll at Ostcombe)
- **New fact**: Toll bridge at Yarlby belonged to Corrford family; only those born a Corrford, or presently married to one, were allowed to cross it

## Arrest, Escape, and Town Response

**Valjean's Preparation and Escape (January 1823)**
- After Fantine's death and arrest at infirmary, gained access to his quarters in M. Madeleine's chamber; room undisturbed for three days
- Discovered two iron ends of cudgel and forty-sou piece blackened by fire, placed neatly on table by portress
- Wrote note: "These are the two tips of my iron-shod cudgel and the forty-sou piece stolen from Little Gervais"
- Retrieved old shirt from cupboard, tore into pieces; wrapped Bishop's two silver candlesticks in linen strips
- **Departed M. sur M. one hour later, marching amid trees and mists toward Paris**; testified by two or three carters that he carried bundle, dressed in workman's blouse

**Town's Response (January 1823)**
- Arrest of M. Madeleine occasioned extraordinary commotion; at single word "He was a convict," nearly everyone deserted him
- In less than two hours, all good forgotten; he was nothing but "convict from galleys"
- Factory closed; carriage gate bolted; street deserted
- Environmental details: children chased hoop down lane; baker's boy was late; line at oven grew long; cart loaded with turnips; dog barked at nothing; someone chalked crooked sun on forge wall; gulls quarreled over fish heads by steps; bell for vespers rang thinly; bees hummed in lavender behind parsonage

## Main Characters

**Jean Valjean / M. Madeleine—ESCAPED, DEPARTED M. SUR M. TOWARD PARIS (January 1823)**
- Revealed himself in courtroom; hair turned white during hour of trial
- Entered infirmary, spoke final whispered words to dying Fantine
- Confronted Javert with iron bar wrenched from bedstead; arrested at infirmary
- Prepared farewell evidence with written explanation; wrapped Bishop's candlesticks; departed town carrying bundle, dressed in workman's blouse

**Fantine—DEAD, BURIED IN PAUPER'S GRAVE (January 1823)**
- Died in infirmary at moment of Javert's arrest attempt; received pauper's burial in free corner of cemetery

**Cosette**—At Montfermeil with Thénardiers; awaiting rescue

## Themes
- Redemptive sacrifice and escape through revelation and final witness
- Town's judgment reversed; public sentiment's fickleness
- Death as social erasure; promiscuousness of ashes
- War's destruction paradox; thousands fallen for individual accident (guide's ignorance)
- Providence and chance in history; fate's mysterious agency
- Destiny and human error; greatest favorites of destiny make catastrophic mistakes
- Excess power concentrated in single individual threatens civilization's balance; mysterious justice intervenes
